title: AI Fire and the Future of Thinking
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau argues that AI in schools should be understood through the analogy of fire: like fire, AI is neither good nor bad in itself but dangerous when uncontrolled, and the productive question is not whether to allow it but how to harness and govern it. Fire transformed human civilization — enabling cooking, heating, tool-making, and social life organized around the hearth — but only when controlled; uncontrolled, it is indiscriminate and destructive. Didau contends that both the utopian view (AI will democratize expertise and personalize learning) and the dystopian view (AI is a cheating engine and existential threat to thought) contain partial truths but are too simplistic. Of particular concern is not AI making things wrong but making things merely faster — accelerating the production of resources, reports, and plans that look impressive while requiring no genuine thinking from anyone. The article then presents five research findings as a structured warning system: students know there is a cost to AI use but use it anyway; students who use AI best are those who need it least; the best AI tutors are deliberately obstructive; AI can strengthen participation or replace it; and the better AI gets, the more human judgment matters. Together, these findings yield a simple test: AI is useful when it helps students think more clearly and become less dependent on AI — harmful when it substitutes for thinking rather than sharpening it.
points: The fire analogy reframes the AI debate from a binary pro/con argument into a governance question: uncontrolled AI is dangerous, but the correct response is controlled use, not prohibition or uncritical adoption.

AI accelerating already-hollow activities — generating resources that look good without requiring thought, writing reports without engaging with classroom reality — is potentially more damaging than AI used for outright cheating, because it is harder to identify.

The finding that students who use AI best need it least reveals an equity trap: AI tools may primarily benefit already-proficient students, widening rather than closing the gaps they are sometimes promoted as solving.

The best AI tutors being 'deliberately obstructive' challenges the intuitive design goal of making AI more helpful and fluent — productive friction, not frictionless compliance, is what drives learning.
The practical test for any AI use in school: does this help students think more clearly and become less dependent on AI over time? If the answer is no, the use should be questioned or redesigned.
quotes: No-one is pro-fire or anti-fire. We're pro-hearth and anti-arson. In a kiln, a furnace, or a carefully managed campfire, fire is wonderful. But obviously, no one wants it in the curtains, the wastepaper bin or the roof space. The question isn't whether fire is useful but how its power is harnessed and how its risks are managed.
AI will make some things in schools better, some things worse and quite a lot of things merely faster. That last possibility should worry us more than it does.

Schools are already full of tasks that can be completed without anyone thinking very much. Just as students can copy notes without understanding them, teachers can produce resources that look attractive but don't teach anything particularly well.

AI hasn't created these problems — they stem from all-too-human desires to save time, avoid effort and look good — but it has accelerated them. And, as with fire, pouring accelerant over a poorly controlled system is never a good bet.

For some, AI is about to democratise expertise, personalise learning, solve workload and make every child's education infinitely adaptive. For others, it's a cheating engine, a hallucination machine and an existential threat to thought itself. Both responses contain some truth, but both are too simplistic.
It's pointless to discuss whether AI should be allowed into education — it's here, baby! The real question is whether we can control it and what we need to guard against.
